papers.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture
papers.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. papers.title: Adaptive Mutual–Human Reflection: A Universal Framework for Multi-LLM Reciprocal Reflection, Human Metacognitive Participation, and Context-Aware Switching
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly employ reflection mechanisms to inspect their own outputs, identify potential errors, reconsider intermediate decisions, and improve subsequent responses. Recent research has also demonstrated the potential of multi-agent debate, collaborative critique, and human feedback for improving the quality of artificial intelligence systems. However, reflection in intelligent systems remains substantially fragmented across self-reflection, multi-agent interaction, external evaluation, and human feedback. In particular, an important architectural question remains: should a system rely on reciprocal reflection among multiple LLMs, human reflection, or a dynamically coordinated combination of both, and how should it determine when to transition between these mechanisms? This paper introduces Adaptive Mutual–Human Reflection (AMHR), a theoretical framework developed as a function-specific extension of the Universal Mutual-Human Model (UMHM). AMHR establishes two fundamental reflection dimensions: Mutual Reflection (M), in which two or more distinct LLMs reciprocally examine, challenge, interpret, and revise one another's reasoning and conclusions; and Human Reflection (H), in which human individuals or groups independently examine and reconsider the assumptions, reasoning, evidence, judgments, and outcomes of an intelligent system. papers.title: From reproducibility to comparability in computational photochemistry: lessons from the PhotoChem explorer prototype
papers.summary: We present the PhotoChem Explorer (PCE) prototype, a proof-of-concept web-based platform that represents computational photochemistry studies of gas-phase molecules in a structured and queryable form. Rather than treating excited-state dynamics simulations as isolated results reported in heterogeneous formats and across different sources, PCE organizes studies according to their molecular systems, computational workflows, methodological choices, and associated observables, facilitating that relationships and trends can be explored systematically across studies. In this way, the prototype illustrates how structured data representations could support improved findability, comparison, reproducibility, and reuse in computational photochemistry. At a fundamental level, it demonstrates how excited-state dynamics studies could become part of a more connected and cumulative body of knowledge, potentially enabling new modes of investigation. The prototype exposes practical challenges that must be addressed to realize this vision, including the development of shared representations, workflow descriptions, and their integration into scientific practice. More broadly, PCE is intended as a practice-driven experimentation platform to stimulate discussion and iterative community development of standards and representations for excited-state dynamics studies.

papers.title: Responsible AI Governance in Iran: A Program-Theory Evaluation of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence has become a strategic technology whose development requires coordinated institutional, regulatory, ethical, and infrastructural governance. This study evaluated the capacity of Iran’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy to support responsible AI governance by reconstructing its underlying program theory and examining the coherence of its implementation architecture. The research adopted a qualitative, theory-based case-study design. Data were obtained through documentary analysis of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and related policy materials, together with semi-structured interviews with 12 experts from academic, research, policy, and industrial backgrounds. The data were coded and thematically analysed using MAXQDA, after which an integrated theory of change and theory of action was developed and applied to the national strategy. The findings indicated that responsible AI governance in Iran depends on sustained political commitment, a legally empowered and agile coordinating institution, equitable access to high-quality data and computational infrastructure, interdisciplinary human capital, effective university–industry collaboration, risk-based regulation, and continuous policy evaluation. The strategy provides an important normative foundation by emphasizing human dignity, national values, scientific development, priority sectors

papers.title: A roadmap for polymer informatics superintelligence
papers.summary: Polymer informatics has matured from isolated property-prediction studies into an integrated discipline that couples data, models, and decision-making across the polymer design cycle. Yet it still falls short of a true intelligent system capable of inverse design on demand, causal reasoning across chemistry, processing, and performance, and closed-loop autonomous experimentation. This article traces a roadmap toward that goal, grounded in experience developing two complementary agentic and informatics platforms. Central to this vision is a modular, agent-directed architecture in which a polymer superintelligence layer interprets a researcher’s design question in natural language and coordinates domain-specialized tools, matched to the available data, for neat polymers, composites and formulations, solvents, and synthesis and processing. The resulting system spans the full chain from molecular design through processing to product-level performance and human perception. Orchestrated together, its generative design, synthesis-feasibility reasoning, and practicality assessment already form the decision-making core of a self-driving polymer laboratory, leaving autonomous, closed-loop experimentation as the principal step that remains. papers.title: NeuroImgAgent: a multi-agent platform for cross-species fMRI analysis with evidence-gated quality control
papers.summary: Cross-species functional MRI analysis requires coordinating specialized workflows and assessing intermediate outputs. We present NeuroImgAgent, a multi-agent platform driven by large language models that translates natural-language requests into workflows for humans, macaques, rats and mice. Quantitative checks and vision-language model assessments determine whether processing continues, enters bounded recovery or stops. Across 268 paired cases, preprocessing metrics were broadly comparable to those of fMRIPrep, AFNI and RABIES. With GPT-5.5, NeuroImgAgent corrected 111 of 120 induced orientation errors and passed all 52 intent-recognition and planning tasks, 8 of 9 recovery tasks and 11 of 14 tool-construction tasks on NeuroAgentBench. In 120 paired challenge cases, the full configuration increased usability from 76.7% to 92.5%, as assessed by blinded experts, and reduced unusable outputs delivered without warning from 18.3% to 4.2% of cases relative to quality-control ablation.

papers.title: Llama-Polya: Instruction Tuning for Large Language Model Based on Polya’s Problem-Solving

papers.title: Independent Learning after Generative AI Support in School Mathematics: A Systematic Review and Assessment-Stratified Meta-Analysis
papers.summary: Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence: Competencies for design in emerging creative environments
papers.summary: The study, titled From Artificial Intelligence: Competencies for Design in Emerging Creative Environments, aims to determine the competencies linked to the use of Artificial Intelligence in the training of designers, as well as to examine its impact on the professional environment. The advancement of AI has reconfigured not only the tools for design practice, but also the essential dynamics of the creative process. In emerging human-AI collaboration [HAIC] scenarios, these systems operate as cooperative agents and not merely as support tools. However, even though design students are progressively incorporating these technologies into their practice, a gap persists in the development of fundamental competencies for establishing effective interaction with these systems. Therefore, the need to strengthen disciplinary training through competencies that integrate critical interpretation, collaborative interaction, ethical and metacognitive reflection, in addition to specialized technical mastery is recognized. Based on the above, this research is structured around a comprehensive review of scientific literature, analysing studies retrieved from specialized databases in both design and higher education. The methodology will adopt the PRISMA [2021] systematic review protocol, which will ensure a rigorous process for the identification, selection, and synthesis of emerging competencies

papers.title: When Human Assurance Matters: Task Complexity and Pre-Interaction Expected Satisfaction in Human-AI Hybrid Service Systems
papers.summary: Consumers frequently disengage from AI service encounters because they doubt whether chatbots can resolve their requests. Although human–AI hybrid systems provide human backup, this capability is often concealed. Drawing on Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Cognitive Appraisal Theory, we examine when human assurance—an upfront statement that users may transfer to a human if the AI cannot resolve the request—improves pre-interaction expectations. A between-subjects online experiment (N = 217) and a within-subject EEG experiment (N = 35) show that assurance increases expected system capability and expected satisfaction, with larger effects under high task complexity. Expected system capability mediates this relationship. EEG results reveal early frontal theta synchronization followed by later frontal alpha desynchronization under high complexity, a temporal pattern consistent with affective engagement and cognitive elaboration. These findings identify human assurance as a task-contingent cue that makes hybrid systems’ recourse capability visible.

papers.title: Reconstructing The Concept Of Self Actualisation In Artificial Intelligence Based Learning : An Integrative Literature Review
papers.summary: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the learning ecology by positioning AI as a cognitive partner that supports personalisation, feedback, problem-solving, and creativity. This transformation necessitates a reconstruction of the concept of self-actualisation, as some human cognitive activities can be delegated to AI. This study aims to analyse the transformation of self actualisation, identify the conditions that strengthen or hinder it, and formulate a conceptual framework for self-actualisation in AI-based learning. This study employs a qualitative library research approach using an integrative literature review design. The findings indicate that GenAI is paradoxical in nature: it can serve as a cognitive scaffold that strengthens autonomy, competence, self-regulation, creativity, metacognition, and epistemic agency, while also potentially encouraging cognitive offloading, dependence, and the weakening of cognitive autonomy. This study proposes the Reflective-Relational Self Actualisation Framework in AI Learning Ecologies (RRSA-AILE), which encompasses autonomy, competence, relatedness, epistemic agency, metacognitive reflexivity, generative creativity, and ethical responsibility. Theoretically, RRSA-AILE integrates humanism, Self-Determination Theory, Self-Regulated Learning, and learner agency. Practically, the framework provides a

papers.title: EgoPlay: Event-Triggered Video Editing for Egocentric Streams
papers.summary: We introduce EgoPlay, an event-triggered video-to-video editor for egocentric streams, obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained V2V diffusion transformer on event-conditioned data built primarily from Ego4D. Given a monocular video and an event-triggered prompt of the form “when X happens, do Y,” EgoPlay infers whether and when event X occurs, preserves pre-event frames, and applies edit Y only to the post-event continuation. Rather than cascading a separate event detector with an editor, EgoPlay learns event recognition, temporal restraint, and pixel-level editing jointly in a single end-to-end model, while also handling negative and multi-event prompts. To support this, we construct a large-scale dataset of 106K event-triggered clip–prompt pairs spanning positive triggers, fabricated-trigger negatives, and multi-event prompts. We then train a bidirectional video diffusion editor with event-triggered supervision and derive a causal variant for chunk-by-chunk streamable inference. We further introduce an event-aware evaluation protocol that separately measures post-trigger editing quality, pre-trigger preservation, and false-trigger robustness. On the Ego4D benchmark, EgoPlay substantially outperforms EgoEdit, the state-of-the-art instruction-based egocentric video editing baseline, with relative gains of 17.7%, 16.9%, and 16.4% in editing quality, visual quality, and background co

papers.title: The Governance Frontier COBIT-Aligned AI Decision Support and Risk-Adaptive Optimization for Enterprise Technology Modernization
papers.summary: Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacy-system transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, opera-tional, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a risk-adaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preference-information triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we compu-tationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmark-ing against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. A systematic review of university and public-sector governance, with observational process-log anal

papers.title: Human-first learning: scaffolding reasoning before AI assistance improves diagnostic accuracy
papers.summary: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). papers.title: Lived experiences of relationships to generative AI mental health chatbots among adults
papers.summary: Nigeria’s mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human es

papers.title: A Brick in the Creative Wall: The Cultural and Creative Production System Facing the Challenge of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly transforming cultural and creative industries (CCIs), yet research lacks a structured understanding of how they intervene across production processes. How and where does GenAI reshape value creation activities within the CCI production system? Building on the UNESCO cultural cycle (2009), we develop an analytical framework that maps GenAI applications across three phases of the cultural production value chain: creation, production, and distribution/consumption. It identifies how GenAI reconfigures value creation and value capture mechanisms differently across phases and sectors. Our analysis highlights emerging dynamics, including phase-specific technological dependencies, increasing feedback loops between production and consumption, and a growing technological convergence across CCIs. To illustrate these mechanisms, we present cases from Galleries, Libraries, Archives and Museums (GLAM). Our paper contributes to ongoing debates on digital transformation in cultural production systems, providing insights for researchers, policymakers, and cultural organizations navigating the opportunities and risks of GenAI. JEL Codes: H0, M0, M1, O4

papers.title: Bridging the intention–behavior gap in psychologically informed musculoskeletal rehabilitation: A con-vergent mixed-methods investigation and the triadic care model

papers.title: Adapting HR Strategies to Enhance CRM in Aviation: A Qualitative Study on Emerging Technologies Grounded in Socio-Technical Systems Theory
papers.summary: Purpose –This study aims to explore how Human Resource Management (HRM) strategies can enhance Crew Resource Management (CRM) effectiveness in the context of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) in aviation. While these technologies improve operational efficiency, they also highlight the critical need for maintaining human oversight and decision-making processes.Design/methodology/approach –The research employs a qualitative methodology grounded in Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory. Data were collected through interviews with 15 aviation experts, including pilots, HR professionals, and operations managers, and analyzed using thematic analysis with NVivo software.Results–The findings indicate that while automation significantly enhances operational efficiency, maintaining manual skills and human decision-making remains essential for sustainable operations. The study also identifies the need for HR strategies to adapt to technological change through enhanced training programs, continuous learning initiatives, and revised recruitment practices.Discussion –This study contributes to STS theory by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological and social systems to ensure effective CRM in aviation. Practical recommendations for HR strategies are provided, including improving training programs, fosteringa culture of continuous

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Discovering High Level Patterns from Simulation Traces
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are unable to reliably reason about specific physical systems. Attempts to imbue LLMs with knowledge of the necessary physics concepts have shown great promise, but explainability and validation remain open challenges. An emerging alternative is tooling, where LLMs can query physical simulators and use the resulting simulation traces as context for validation. This approach suffers from poor scalability since simulation traces contain large volumes of fine-grained numerical and semantic data. We show that translating simulation traces to a sparse representation of ‘high-level’ structural patterns leads to more effective interpretation by LLMs. We propose an unsupervised learning scheme to perform this translation, or annotation, via program synthesis. Our learning results in a library of programs that act as pattern detectors which can translate simulation logs to sparse, annotated pattern sequences. The detected patterns may optionally be guided by human experts via string labels (rigid collision, stretching spring, etc.). We show, using a recent physics benchmark, that such annotated representations are more amenable to natural language reasoning about specific physical systems. The synthesised programs serve as transparent, explainable functions that map system states to a sparse and efficient annotation space. As an example application, we show

papers.title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
papers.summary: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest , an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.

papers.title: Support systems used by students at an open distance e-learning university
papers.summary: Introduction The problem and purpose of the study. Student support and wellbeing remain understudied in South African higher education distance e-learning. Distance e-learning students are socially, academically, and geographically isolated and often have limited access to wellbeing support. As a result, students may rely on external support to manage their wellbeing. Methods Design, participants, data collection and analysis. Guided by the Socioecological model, this paper examines the support systems that distance e-learning students use to manage their wellbeing. A qualitative descriptive research design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with students enrolled at a distance-learning institution in South Africa, recruited through purposive sampling. Results The main findings. Using reflexive thematic analysis, a multidimensional support for wellbeing was identified among students in a distance e-learning context. Five support elements were derived from the findings: family support for emotional wellbeing; peer relationships for wellbeing; spiritual support through religious institutions and meaning-making; institutional support for wellbeing; and community health system support and physical activity. The integration of these five elements of support was critical for the wellbeing of distance e-learning students. Discussion What the findings mean and their implica

papers.title: From Algorithmic Control to Learner-Driven Personalisation: Rethinking AI in Education
papers.summary: AI-driven personalised learning now shapes the pace, practice, and feedback of millions of learners. Most systems, however, personalise learning for the learner through opaque algorithmic decisions instead of equipping learners to personalise their own study. This review examines that asymmetry. Twenty-five studies published between 2017 and 2026, retrieved from Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus, are synthesised thematically around learner agency, self-regulated learning, and system design. The synthesis identifies an illusion of autonomy: surface-level choices sit alongside algorithmic authority over goals, sequencing, and mastery criteria, which narrows the room learners have to practise goal setting, strategic monitoring, and reflective evaluation. Duolingo and two platforms used in Vietnam serve as illustrative cases showing how gamified metrics and default pathways can redirect attention from meaningful goals towards externally driven engagement. The paper answers with a learner-driven personalisation framework resting on three principles: shared control, design that activates self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency coupled with AI literacy. A three-item rubric operationalises the framework so that schools can detect illusion-of-autonomy risks before adoption. The analysis extends to equity, since learners with limited devices, connectivity, or AI literacy gai

papers.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI
papers.summary: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

A Hybrid Deep Learning Framework Based on ResNet and Vision Transformer for Pneumonia Detection from Chest X-ray Images
papers.summary: Pneumonia continues to pose a serious threat to global health, particularly in low-resource settings where timely diagnosis is challenging. To address limitations in both feature extraction and contextual understanding of chest X-ray (CXR) images, we propose a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a customized Residual Neural Network (ResNet) with a Vision Transformer (ViT). Unlike prior works that merely fuse convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers, our architecture introduces a feature fusion strategy that leverages the local spatial encoding capabilities of ResNet and the global self-attention mechanism of ViT in a complementary and optimized manner. Evaluated on benchmark CXR datasets, the proposed ResNet-ViT model achieves an accuracy of 97.03%, with marked improvements in sensitivity and specificity compared to standalone CNN or transformer models. Furthermore, attention visualization highlights critical pneumonia-affected regions, offering clinical interpretability. This hybrid model not only enhances diagnostic performance but also shows potential for deployment in real-world clinical decision support systems, especially in resource-constrained environments.
